ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Generalization and Hallucination Mechanisms in LLMs through Gradient-Based Training Dynamics
PROPOSAL: Derive a theoretical framework that explains how gradient-based training dynamics in transformers enable them to infer implications for subjects whose implications were never observed during training.
CONTROLS: Compare to a transformer trained without gradients for the relevant inference pathway.
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This theoretical framework will provide a clear explanation for how and when gradients enable generalization in LLMs, helping to distinguish between generalization and hallucination mechanisms. The model's performance without gradients will likely lack generalization, but may avoid hallucination.

This proposal sets the stage for a theoretical investigation of gradient-based training in LLMs, allowing us to better understand the representation learning dynamics that enable these models to generalize beyond their training data.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Evaluation of Factual Knowledge Inference
PROPOSAL: Design and train a suite of synthetic experiments using a graspable knowledge graph, where the learning objectives and evaluation metrics are carefully controlled to isolate various aspects of factual knowledge inference, such as implications, inferences, and hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Compare different training procedures (e.g., matching, adversarial), architectural choices (e.g., different number of layers), and evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall, accuracy) to identify key factors influencing generalization and hallucination.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: These controlled experiments will reveal how various components of the model and training procedure interact to produce generalization and hallucination. However, the models might still fail to generalize perfectly due to simulation limitations, but gains in identifying critical factors influencing hallucination could be possible.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Synthetic Evaluation of Factual Knowledge Inference
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Design and train a suite of synthetic experiments using a graspable knowledge graph, where the learning objectives and evaluation metrics are carefully controlled to isolate various aspects of factual knowledge inference, such as implications, inferences, and hallucinations. To reduce simulation limitations, incorporate domain-specific datatypes (e.g. times, dates, locations, amounts) to simulate "realistic" abstract inference operations in the graph with minimal ambiguity.
CONTROLS: Same as before
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised setup should improve actual equity in inference for most relationship types or whole data tasks tested.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Synthetic Evaluation of Factual Knowledge Inference
PROPOSAL: REVISED: Design and train a suite of synthetic experiments using a graspable knowledge graph, where the learning objectives and evaluation metrics are carefully controlled to isolate various aspects of factual knowledge inference, such as implications, inferences, and hallucinations. To reduce simulation limitations, incorporate domain-specific datatypes (e.g. times, dates, locations, amounts) to simulate "realistic" abstract inference operations in the graph with minimal ambiguity.
CONTROLS: Compare different training procedures (e.g., matching, adversarial), architectural choices (e.g., different number of layers), and evaluation metrics (e.g., precision, recall, accuracy) to identify key factors influencing generalization and hallucination.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This revised setup should improve actual equity in inference for most relationship types or whole data tasks tested, with better outcomes in terms of Hallucinations reduction.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Impact of Different Inference Pathways on Generalization and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Investigate how different inference pathways, such as monotonic, counterfactual, and probabilistic inference, affect a model's ability to generalize and hallucinate in the context of factual knowledge inference.
CONTROLS: Compare performance across different inference pathways and selection methods on a set of controlled tasks from the graspable knowledge graph.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This analysis will provide insight into the specific factors contributing to generalization and hallucination, and could inform strategies to improve performance in one aspect while mitigating the other. However, the models might need careful training to quickly select the correct path, if exact perfect performance expected on that.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Mitigating Hallucinations through Input-Output Regularization
PROPOSAL: Investigate the effectiveness of input-output regularization techniques, such as injective and surjective training objectives, in reducing hallucinations while maintaining generalization in LLMs.
CONTROLS: Compare regularized models to baselines trained without regularization on a set of real-world factual knowledge inference tasks.
COST: 40 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This approach might significantly improve the model's ability to avoid hallucinations, but could potentially come at a cost to generalization if not carefully tuned. The actual impact may vary based on task type and domain of use.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Attention Mechanisms in Factual Knowledge Inference
PROPOSAL: Analyze how attention mechanisms in LLMs contribute to generalization and hallucination during factual knowledge inference, and investigate techniques to control attention for improved performance.
CONTROLS: Compare different attention-weighting schemes, attention mechanisms (e.g., fixed, learnable, combination), and attention control techniques (e.g., regularization, masking) on a set of real-world factual knowledge inference tasks.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By understanding the role of attention mechanisms, we can develop targeted techniques to improve model performance, reducing hallucinations and maintaining generalization. However, attention masking techniques could potentially harm model generalization if not carefully implemented.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Factual Knowledge Transfer from Pretrained LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the extent to which factual knowledge is transferred from a pretrained LLM to a fine-tuned model on a specific downstream task, focusing on implications for generalization and hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the transferred knowledge to that acquired through fine-tuning from scratch, and evaluate performance on a set of factual knowledge inference tasks after knowledge transfer.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This evaluation will provide insight into how LLMs acquire and transfer factual knowledge, possibly shedding light on the relationship between pretraining and hallucination. However, the models may need specific hyperparameter tuning, adapting learning procedures & knowledge resolver to most successful result during evaluation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Developing a Formal Model for Factual Knowledge Inference in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Derive a formal model that captures the key factors and processes involved in factual knowledge inference in LLMs, potentially combining framework elements from gradient-based training dynamics and inference pathway analysis.
CONTROLS: Validate the formal model by comparing its predictions to empirical results from the existing experiments (proposals 1-6).
COST: 100 GPU-hours (theoretical modeling and validation)
PREDICTION: This formal model will provide a unified understanding of the mechanisms underlying factual knowledge inference, enabling the development of more effective methods for reducing hallucinations while maintaining generalization. However, the actual complexity of real-world LLM's will require specifically addressing and inhibition individual components and potentially sacrificing complete predictive functionality.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Real-World Validation of Factual Knowledge Inference Methods
PROPOSAL: Implement and evaluate the most promising methods for reducing hallucinations while maintaining generalization on real-world factual knowledge inference tasks, using a diverse set of benchmark datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the developed methods to state-of-the-art models on the benchmark datasets, and assess their robustness and adaptability to different domains and tasks.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (large-scale real-world experiments)
PREDICTION: This real-world evaluation will provide a comprehensive assessment of the effectiveness of the developed methods in practical scenarios, and will help to identify areas for further improvement. However, the models might need more robust and efficient architectures and hyperparameters to extend their ability beyond current benchmarks' capabilities.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Propagation of Gradient Updates During Factual Knowledge Injection
PROPOSAL: We study how gradient updates during fine-tuning propagate through the LLM, focusing on the interaction between learned representations and the newly injected facts. We analyze the gradient flow through the model's embeddings, self-attention weights, and output layers to understand how gradients from factual knowledge affect the model's overall representation.
CONTROLS: Analyze the gradient flow separately for factually correct and incorrect fine-tuning scenarios.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to find that gradient updates from factual knowledge primarily affect the neural representations for the subject, relation, and answer slots, rather than the model's global representation. Hallucination could be attributed to the lack of regularization on these neural representations during fine-tuning. However, this analysis may fail to identify the underlying mechanisms for strong generalization, as the gradient flow analysis alone may overlook the model's potential for forming unobserved connections during training.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Data Generation for Evaluating Factual Knowledge Generalization
PROPOSAL: We design and generate a large synthetic dataset of facts and their implications, covering a variety of relational facts and entities. This dataset allows us to control the train and test split, enabling a thorough evaluation of a model's ability to generalize and hallucinate after fine-tuning. Specifically, the dataset will include triples (s, r, a) and additional triples (s, r_1, a_i) that imply (s, r_2, c_i), with varying relationships (r_1, r_2) and entities (s, a, a_i, c_i).
CONTROLS: Evaluate the impact of dataset size, structure, and diversity on the model's generalization and hallucination performance.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the synthetic dataset will allow us to baseline a model's performance on various factual generalization tasks, and observe that the hallucination rate decreases as the dataset size and structural diversity increase. However, we may find that the model's performance on generalization tasks deteriorates as a consequence of overfitting to the synthetic data, which could limit the external validity of our findings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Implication-Directed Training for LLMs
PROPOSAL: We propose an alternative training objective that encourages the model to explicitly reason about implications from given facts. This is achieved by introducing a secondary loss term that rewards the model for predicting correct implications from the given facts. For example, given the fact (s, lives in, Paris), the model would predict (s, speaks, French), (s, has a French accent, True), etc.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our implication-directed training objective against various baselines, including standard fine-tuning and existing works on distant supervision or sequence-to-sequence reasoning.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect implication-directed training to reduce hallucination rates while maintaining or improving generalization capabilities. However, this proposal may fail to explore the optimal way of incorporating the implication loss term into the training objective, potentially leading to suboptimal performance.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Refining Implication-Directed Training for LLMs
PROPOSAL: We revisit the implication-directed training objective (REV 3) and refine it by incorporating a lagged implication loss term. The new objective also rewards the model for predicting the implications of the factual knowledge at multiple steps in the future, similar to how humans reason about real-world events. For instance, given the fact (s, lives in, Paris) and the implication (s, speaks, French), the model would predict the further implication (s, has a French restaurant, nearby). This lagged loss would allow the model to better capture relationships between seemingly unrelated entities and events.
CONTROLS: Maintain the same baselines as before and compare the performance of the refined objective against it.
COST: 120 GPU-hours (expect it to converge faster with the additional regularization from the old objective)
PREDICTION: The refined implication-directed training should improve the model's generalization capabilities and outperform existing baselines. However, we risk exacerbating overfitting due to the increased model capacity required to capture complex relationships.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Socio-Causal Graph Analysis for Factual Knowledge Understanding
PROPOSAL: We introduce a socio-causal graph (SCG) to analyze and visualize the relationships between facts, implications, and entities in the synthetic dataset. The SCG is a directed graph where nodes represent entities, and edges represent the causal relationships between them. By analyzing the graph structure and topology, we can identify key subgraphs and graph motifs associated with hallucinations and correct generalizations.
CONTROLS: Examine the network properties of the SCG for both real and synthesized networks to better understand its characteristics. Evaluate the relationship between the graph properties and the model's hallucination rate.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the SCG analysis will reveal common patterns and structures that are more likely to lead to hallucinations or correct generalizations. However, depending on the model's ability to generalize, the SCG may not be able to capture all the complex relationships inherent in factual knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Provable Initialization of LLM Embeddings for Factual Knowledge
PROPOSAL: Building on the gradient propagation analysis (PROPOSAL 1), we develop a novel initialization procedure for the LLM embeddings that ensures correct factual knowledge is represented accurately. Our procedure involves pre-training the embeddings on a small subset of the synthetic dataset, such that the resulting embeddings are provably informative about the relationships between entities and facts. This initialization is then used as a starting point for the subsequent fine-tuning process.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of our initialized embeddings against randomized or pre-trained embeddings from other LLMs.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (for pre-training and evaluation)
PREDICTION: We expect our initialized embeddings to lead to improved generalization performance and reduced hallucination rates, as they provide a more accurate basis for the subsequent fine-tuning process. However, our analysis may reveal situations where human-designed pre-training data leads to embeddings too specialized to non-verbal reasoning (potholes as entities) for example.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating the Role of Attention Mechanism in Hallucination
PROPOSAL: We investigate the attention mechanism's influence on hallucination and generalization in the LLM. Specifically, we analyze and compare the attention patterns for correct and incorrect predictions, identifying areas where the attention mechanism tends to deviate from accurate reasoning. We then experiment with attention-based regularization techniques to mitigate hallucination.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of our attention-based regularization against various LLM models, including those without attention mechanisms.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect attention-based regularization to improve model performance and reduce hallucination rates. However, over-regulating the attention mechanism may have a negative impact on the model's overall performance. As the LLM inherits the narrow focus from the fine-tuning task (no paradoxical reasoning deterministically happens after fine-tuning which would focus all attention).

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Unseen Implications through Multi-Step Reasoning
PROPOSAL: We extend the implication-directed training objective (REFINED IMP 3) to a multi-step reasoning framework. Given a sequence of facts, the model predicts subsequent implications, refining its knowledge step-by-step. This approach allows the model to learn more complex relationships between facts and better capture context-dependent implications.
CONTROLS: Compare the performance of the multi-step reasoning framework against other LLMs that have been trained on similar datasets and evaluate its ability to handle long-range dependencies.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect the multi-step reasoning framework to improve the model's ability to identify unseen implications and reduce hallucination rates. However, this approach may be computationally expensive, and we may need to address potential overfitting issues by adding regularization techniques.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Theoretical Analysis of Generalization and Hallucination in LLMs
PROPOSAL: We develop a theoretical framework to understand the relationship between generalization and hallucination in LLMs. Building on the gradient propagation analysis (PROPOSAL 1) and implication-directed training (REFINED IMP 3), we derive bounds on the model's error rates and provide insights into the mechanisms driving hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare our theoretical results against empirical findings from previous proposals.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical work)
PREDICTION: We expect our theoretical framework to provide a solid understanding of the underlying mechanisms driving generalization and hallucination in LLMs. However, the theoretical framework may not fully capture the complexity of the real-world data and the model's behavior, potentially leading to discrepancies between our analysis and empirical results.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Combining Predictive Models for Factual Knowledge Injection Evaluation
PROPOSAL: We propose a meta-learning approach that combines the results of different predictive models (gradient updates, implication-directed training, attention mechanism analysis, and multi-step reasoning) to evaluate the effectiveness of factual knowledge injection. This approach leverages the strengths of each model, reducing reliance on a single method and providing a more comprehensive assessment of the LLM's knowledge acquisition abilities.
CONTROLS: Evaluate the performance of the meta-learning approach against existing state-of-the-art methods on various factual knowledge injection tasks.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (computational complexity is of order O(n*p*M), where n is number of methods)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the meta-learning approach will provide a robust and accurate evaluation metric for factual knowledge injection, improving over individual models in certain scenarios. However, we risk encountering issues with over-combination, where the interdependence between predictive models violates assumptions used in the original designs, which may stain certain designs in isolation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Hallucination and Generalization in Fine-Tuned LLMs: A Synthetic Dataset and Model Analysis
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic dataset of (s, r, a) triples, where s is a subject, r a relation and a an answer, with specific (fact, implication) pairs designed to test for both hallucination and generalization after fine-tuning. Use this dataset to fine-tune a pre-trained LLM and analyze the resulting model's performance on the original (fact, implication) pairs and related questions that require generalization. 
CONTROLS: Compare the fine-tuned model against a pre-trained LLM without fine-tuning, as well as a randomly initialized model.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The fine-tuned model will demonstrate both improved generalization capabilities (e.g., correctly deducing implications) and increased hallucination (e.g., providing factually incorrect answers), with the exact extent of each depending on the specifics of the dataset and fine-tuning regime.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Role of Induction Heads in LLMs
PROPOSAL: Investigate the role of induction heads in LLMs, which have been linked to reasoning behaviors, in enabling both generalization and hallucination after fine-tuning. Apply a perturbation-based technique to selectively remove or modify individual induction heads in a fine-tuned model and evaluate the effect on its performance on (fact, implication) pairs and related questions.
CONTROLS: Compare the results of these perturbations against a model without induction heads, as well as the original fine-tuned model for a baseline.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Removing or modifying induction heads may reduce hallucination by disrupting the model's ability to generate plausible yet incorrect answers, but may also hurt generalization by preventing the model from utilizing relevant patterns and relationships in the training data.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Hallucination and Generalization in Fine-Tuned LLMs: A Synthetic and Real-World Dataset and Model Analysis
PROPOSAL: Extend the synthetic dataset used in proposal 1 to include real-world triples and (fact, implication) pairs, allowing for a more comprehensive evaluation of the model's generalization capabilities and tendency to hallucinate in the context of real-world knowledge. Evaluate the model's performance on the combined synthetic and real-world set.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against the model's performance on the synthetic dataset alone, as well as against a pre-trained LLM without fine-tuning, to gauge the benefit of training on real-world data.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The model will demonstrate increased reliability on real-world (fact, implication) pairs, with reduced hallucination compared to the synthetic dataset alone, but may still struggle with more complex or nuanced implications, highlighting the challenges of fine-tuning for real-world knowledge.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Impact of Training Data Quantity and Quality on Hallucination and Generalization
PROPOSAL: Explore how the quantity and quality of training data affect the model's tendency to hallucinate and its ability to generalize (fact, implication) pairs. Vary the size and diversity of the training set, as well as the specificity and noise levels of the (fact, implication) pairs, to see how these factors influence the model's performance.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a model trained on a fixed, high-quality dataset, to gauge the impact of data quality, and against a model trained on an augmented dataset with additional (fact, implication) pairs, to examine the effect of data quantity.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Increasing the quantity of high-quality training data will improve the model's ability to generalize, but may also increase the likelihood of hallucination if the model becomes over-confident in its predictions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Characterizing the Effect of Attention Patterns on Hallucination and Generalization
PROPOSAL: Investigate how attention patterns in the fine-tuned model relate to its tendency to hallucinate and generalize (fact, implication) pairs. Analyze attention weights to identify patterns that are associated with correct and incorrect generalizations, and examine how these patterns change when the model is fine-tuned on different datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the attention patterns against a pre-trained LLM, to see how fine-tuning affects attention, and against a model with a different attention mechanism, to evaluate the impact of the attention pattern on both generalization and hallucination.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Models that tend to hallucinate will have highly focused attention patterns, concentrated on a few key tokens in the input sequence, while models that can accurately generalize will have more diffuse attention patterns, highlighting relevant relationships between different parts of the input.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding LLMs' Generalization and Hallucination Capabilities
PROPOSAL: Develop a theoretical framework to explain how LLMs generalize and hallucinate (fact, implication) pairs. Specifically, analyze the training dynamics of LLMs and derive a set of constraints that capture the relationship between the model's capacity to learn from training data and its ability to generalize and hallucinate.
CONTROLS: Use mathematical proofs and counterexamples to validate the framework and demonstrate its applicability to different LLM architectures and training regimes.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (purely theoretical work)
PREDICTION: The framework will capture the essence of the relationship between generalization and hallucination, highlighting the role of (fact, implication) pair specificities, induction head strength, attention patterns, and training data quantity and quality in influencing LLM behavior.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: A Theoretical Framework for Understanding LLMs' Generalization and Hallucination Capabilities: Deriving Constraints for Induction Head Strength and Attention Patterns
PROPOSAL: Refine the theoretical framework from proposal 5 by deriving explicit constraints for induction head strength and attention patterns that capture the relationship between these model components and the tendency to generalize or hallucinate (fact, implication) pairs. Specifically, develop mathematical expressions that relate the strength of induction heads to the model's ability to learn from training data and the patterns of attention to the relationships between different parts of the input.
CONTROLS: Use proof-by-contradiction and counterexamples to validate the derived constraints and demonstrate their applicability to different LLM architectures and training regimes.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (purely theoretical work)
PREDICTION: The revised framework will provide a more comprehensive understanding of how LLMs generalize and hallucinate, highlighting the crucial role of induction head strength and attention patterns in influencing the model's behavior, and providing a foundation for future work on designing more robust LLMs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating the Role of Chain-of-Thought Reasoning in LLMs' Generalization and Hallucination
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effect of chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning on LLMs' generalization and hallucination capabilities. Specifically, fine-tune a pre-trained LLM to use a CoT mechanism and compare its performance on (fact, implication) pairs against a baseline model without CoT, and against a model using a different reasoning mechanism (e.g., induction heads).
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a randomly initialized model, to gauge the impact of the CoT mechanism, and against a model trained with a different optimization goal, to evaluate the effect of the reasoning mechanism on LLM behavior.
COST: 120 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Incorporating CoT reasoning will enhance the model's ability to generalize and provide more accurate implications, potentially by encouraging the model to think more explicitly and reasoning about the input sequence. However, CoT might also exacerbate hallucination if the model becomes too confident in its chain of reasoning, particularly if the input is noisy or ambiguous.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Identifying Optimal fine-tuning Strategies for Reducing Hallucination and Enhancing Generalization
PROPOSAL: Conduct a comprehensive search of fine-tuning strategies that emphasize reducing hallucination and enhancing generalization. Specifically, use a Bayesian optimization framework to tuning the fine-tuning objective, the learning rate, the regularization strength, and other relevant hyperparameters to identify the optimal fine-tuning configuration that balances the trade-off between generalization and hallucination.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a model fine-tuned with a fixed set of hyperparameters, to gauge the impact of fine-tuning, and against a pre-trained LLM, to evaluate the benefit of fine-tuning for (fact, implication) pair reasoning.
COST: 250 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The optimal fine-tuning configuration will strike a balance between reducing hallucination and enhancing generalization, highlighted by improved performance on (fact, implication) pairs and reduced tendency to generate factually incorrect answers.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Investigating Hallucination and Generalization in Fine-Tuned LLMs: A Comprehensive Analysis of Synthetic, Real-World, and Robustness Datasets and Model Components
PROPOSAL: Integrate the findings from proposals 2-7 into a comprehensive analysis of the factors that influence LLMs' ability to generalize and hallucinate (fact, implication) pairs. Specifically, evaluate the impact of training data quantity and quality, induction head strength, attention patterns, chain-of-thought reasoning, and optimal fine-tuning strategies on the model's performance on synthetic, real-world, and robustness datasets.
CONTROLS: Compare the results against a pre-trained LLM, to gauge the impact of fine-tuning, and against a model without the key components analyzed in the previous proposals, to evaluate the benefit of each component for (fact, implication) pair reasoning.
COST: 400 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The comprehensive analysis will provide a nuanced understanding of the trade-offs between generalization and hallucination in fine-tuned LLMs, highlighting the importance of a combination of factors, and provide a roadmap for designing more robust and accurate LLMs for (fact, implication) pair reasoning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Investigating Gradient-Based Inference Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: Examine the effect of gradient-based training on the development of inference mechanisms within transformers, focusing on the properties of the model and its training that enable inferring implications for unseen subjects.
CONTROLS: Baseline: train a transformer on a synthetic dataset with no relation between subjects; ablation: remove the gradient updates during training; contrast: train a transformer on a dataset with explicit relation labels.
COST: 50 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Results will show that gradient-based training contributes significantly to the emergence of inference mechanisms, potentially paving the way for understanding why LLMs can also generalise on newly injected factual knowledge. However, it may fail to capture the full complexity of their hallucinations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: Design a synthetic dataset where subjects and implications are explicitly linked, but only a subset of subjects have their implications visible during training. Evaluate a transformer's ability to infer the unseen implications using this dataset, and analyze its performance under different training conditions (e.g., varying the size of the subset).
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a transformer trained on a dataset with no relations between subjects; baseline: compare results to a model trained on a dataset with all implications visible.
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will demonstrate the transformer's capability to learn some form of inference mechanism but the model's ability to generalize may be restricted when only a subset of relations are visible and may fail to generalise when faced with large unseen implications.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: REVISE 2. Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Implication Inference: refine the experiment to specifically study the relationship between the size of the unseen implication set and the model's performance. Train models with varying subset sizes and evaluate their ability to infer the unseen implications. Analyze the impact of increasing the size of the unseen set on the model's ROC-AUC scores and the rate of hallucinations.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a model trained on a dataset with all implications visible; baseline: compare results to a model without any inference mechanism (ORT based baseline).
COST: 40 GPU-hours (due to the refined experiment)
PREDICTION: The experiment will show that both the model's ability to infer implications and hallucinations increase with the size of the unseen set, but their rate of increase may differ. This can provide insight into the relationship between generalization and hallucination in LLMs.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Implication Inference
PROPOSAL: REVISE 2. Synthetic Dataset Analysis for Implication Inference: refine the experiment to specifically study the relationship between the size of the unseen implication set and the model's performance. 

However to add a new analysis to the refined experiment. Study the effect of adding noise to both the fact and implication relations, to see if this can explain the model's hallucinations in unseen implications when not seen during training.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a model trained on a noisy-clean data split, ablation: remove the noisy elements to get a clean model; baseline: compare results to a model that never sees the unseen implications and has relation information noise, this could be a basic synthetic data setup.
COST: 80 GPU-hours (impact of the noisy elements during training)
PREDICTION: This will show whether the noisy information could lead to hallucination errors using unseen implications and whether this also recapitulates the results in the synthetic set from turn 2. But this may fail if noise does not match any real data distribution.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: The Relevance of Implication Heads in Inference Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: Investigate whether the performance difference in inferring implications in unseen subjects is due to the presence of implication heads (the specialized heads used for past, current, and future-time dependencies) in transformers. We analyze the performance of transformers trained on synthetic and real data with and without the implication heads, to see if their presence improves performance on unseen implications.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a transformer without implication heads; AB test: implement premise-question and premise-exclude examples between two models.
COST: 30 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Implication heads likely play a crucial role in a transformer's ability to infer implications, potentially limiting the extent to which a model can generalize beyond the explicitly trained knowledge and also pointing to mechanisms that may be connected to hallucination errors.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: The Relevance of Implication Heads in Inference Mechanisms
PROPOSAL: REVISE 3. The Relevance of Implication Heads in Inference Mechanisms: extend the analysis to study how implication heads influence the rate of hallucinations in the model. Train two iterations of the same model - one with implication heads and another without. Evaluate their respective hallucination rates on unseen implications. Analyze the impact of using implication heads on the model's ability to generalize.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a transformer without implication heads; metric tracking: track rates of reasonable and unreasonable hallucinations separately.
COST: 44 GPU-hours (due to the additional hallucination tracking)
PREDICTION: Results will show whether the implication heads' effect on hallucinations corresponds with their influence on generalization, or whether the model somehow learns to adjust its behavior (hallucinations) in response to the implication heads, potentially explaining why LLMs can be prone to hallucination.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Training Dynamics of Implication Heads
PROPOSAL: Investigate the training dynamics of implication heads in transformers to understand their role in developing inference mechanisms. Analyze the gradient flow and activations within the transformer during training, focusing on the layers containing implication heads. Visualize and quantify their contributions to the transformer's performance on inferring implications.
CONTROLS: Baseline: analyze the training dynamics without implication heads; visualization: use t-SNE, PCA, or other techniques for activations and gradients visualization.
COST: 50 GPU-hours (due to the visualization requirements)
PREDICTION: Insights from this study will provide a deeper understanding of how implication heads contribute to the transformer's ability to infer implications, shedding light on the relationship between the training dynamics and the emergence of inference mechanisms. This may include a nuanced role of implication heads depending on several factors of the training process.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Analyzing the Emergence of Ripple Effects in Transformers
PROPOSAL: Study the emergence of ripple effects – the ability of a model to associate events connected through subjects – in transformers. Design a synthetic dataset where events are connected through shared subjects, and evaluate a transformer's ability to recognize and generalize these connections. Investigate how the model's architecture, training dynamics, and implications heads influence the emergence of ripple effects.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a model without implication heads; baseline: compare results to a model without any connection knowledge.
COST: 60 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: This experiment will provide insights into the transformer's ability to recognize complex connections between events, shedding light on the model's capacity for reasoning and generalization in out-of-context situations, and also potentially providing a mechanistic explanation of why LLMs can generalise so well in many cases.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Understanding the Relationship Between Inference Mechanisms and Hallucinations
PROPOSAL: Investigate the connection between the transformer's inference mechanisms, including implication heads, and its propensity for hallucinations. Design a dataset that requires both inference and generalization, and evaluate the model's performance under conditions that influence the interaction between these mechanisms. This includes manipulating the presence of implication heads, training data, and the task complexity.
CONTROLS: Ablation: compare results to a model without implication heads; baseline: compare results to a model without prior implication heads and without knowledge of relation information; façade control: manipulate the strength of the hallucinations.
COST: 75 GPU-hours
